for leave to introduce Bill No. C-17, to amend the House of Commons Act (internal economy autonomy).
Explain.

The commissioners of internal economy are, apparently, appointed by virtue of the provision of section 16 of the House of Commons Act which provides that there shall be four members of the cabinet plus yourself, Mr. Speaker, to deal with expenditures of money relating to the House of Commons. I understand that this system was originally designed at the time of confederation because of the difficulty of transportation over the distances which many members had to travel in order to get to Ottawa. It was presumably felt that members of the cabinet, who were likely to have their homes in Ottawa, could attend to this work more conveniently.
However, the situation at the moment is that the cabinet itself, by virtue of its majority of four to one compared with Your Honour, has control over monetary and financial matters affecting the House of Commons and it would seem to me that this is not a desirable thing. The bill seeks to remove those provisions in order that the commissioners of internal economy might be selected by the house itself.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED FAILURE TO COLLECT MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Postmaster General. Has the Postmaster General any comment to make in regard to the report in this morning's Gazette to the effect that
6.000	letters had been discovered lying for two weeks in a forgotten mail box?

subtopic: REPORTED FAILURE TO COLLECT MAIL
speechtext:
May I just say, Mr. Speaker, that when I heard the dulcet tones of the hon. member for St. Denis I knew the house was really back in session.
This was a case of mail boxes having been removed from streets during street repairs, when we could not reach them with our trucks. The contractor who was to clear the box was informed by the post office, and through an error in the contractor's organization the chauffeur who drove the truck was not properly informed and therefore the box was not cleared.
This was a considerable annoyance to myself and the Post Office Department. I might point out that we have between 7,000 and
8.000	of these boxes across Canada, each of them being cleared several times a day making a total of perhaps 40,000 clearances. The very fact that this instance has attracted so much attention is proof that our system of control is generally satisfactory and that this is a most exceptional case.
However, it has been my experience that mistakes occur less frequently when they are punished. Since this is clearly the responsibility of the mail contractor concerned, a substantial financial penalty is being levied against the contractor and we have directed him to take disciplinary action against those in his organization who were directly responsible.
As minister, I do not take a disinterested attitude toward failures in our service, nor condone errors when those errors represent carelessness. I think this attitude may in part be responsible for the steady decrease in the number of complaints from the public regarding our service over the last several years.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I want to follow the time honoured and good custom of congratulating the mover, the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages), and the seconder, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne), of the address in reply.
They would not expect me to agree with all the things they said or the arguments they

The Address-Mr. Pearson brought forward but they undoubtedly discharged their task to the satisfaction of their colleagues, and I take it that was their chief objective in discharging this honourable responsibility. I should like also to congratulate them on the skill of their brick-building with the straw that was available to them.
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member who has been appointed Deputy Speaker of the house, and I do that in a very sincere way. I feel sure that he will discharge his important and honourable function with fairness, impartiality and intelligence-those qualities, Mr. Speaker, which you have exhibited to such a high degree in your occupancy of the chair.
I should like to congratulate my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Flynn), on his elevation to the cabinet as Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, and those other hon. members who have been made parliamentary secretaries or have been given other distinctions.
The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys must have been highly flattered by all the publicity given to his appointment to the cabinet. Perhaps, however, his satisfaction in this regard may have been modified by the realization that the attention which was centred on Quebec at this particular time was not exclusively devoted, I feel sure, to his promotion. There is no doubt that more was expected than even this important promotion -especially by the press-because of officially inspired and officially sponsored speculation.
We have in Canada today a government and a Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who seem to enjoy giving birth to speculations and then to destroy their own speculative infants. Hence, Mr. Speaker, the fiasco of the deluxe pilgrimage to Quebec with private cars, aeroplanes and attendant officials, and all the panoply of an expectant press which is so flattering to the ego of ministers. What a circus performance that turned out to be, with a result, I think it is fair to say, that could have been achieved quietly and inexpensively in Ottawa.
What did it all accomplish, in this time of difficulties, deficits and very serious problems? The verdict of one member of the press gallery in connection with the accomplishments of this trip-the parliamentary correspondent of the Globe and Mail-had this to say when writing on January 3 of this year. I quote from Mr. Walter Gray's column:
The attendant publicity, and the Prime Minister's statements over press speculation-which the press maintains was originated by Mr. Dieienbaker himself-has left a cloud of foul air over parliament hill.
As it happened, this double-shuffle ended in a "no deal" and all the ministers sit- though perhaps somewhat less easily-on the

same front benches who were there previously. It was merely another chapter in the record of a government which prefers agitation to administration, surface excitement to sober results.

The minister said in Nova Scotia last December that the delay in calling an election was due to the government's desire to fulfil all its promises before appealing to the people. That is a prediction which would mean an indefinite delay in setting an election date.

The Address-Mr. Pearson
I can understand the desire of hon. gentlemen opposite to wait. Perhaps they are delaying for the same reason as inspired Right Hon. R. B. Bennett to put off his fate until the last moment in 1935. Of course, we must remember that the Prime Minister has always placed great faith in the healing virtues of delay, as in the camouflaging magic of confusion. We on this side believe that an election should be held-that the people of this country should be given a chance to express themselves at the earliest possible date. It should be an election with the full and detailed government program placed before the people, together with a detailed national accounting, so that they would know what has been going on in the country in recent years in order that the people can decide in the light of all the facts. The sooner that comes about in the conditions I have mentioned the better for Canada, though, of course, the worse for this government.
Let me say a few words about the speech from the throne itself. It is not a very ambitious document but I do not intend on this occasion to try to deal with all the references contained in it. My colleagues will deal with some of the proposals and some of the ideas, and I shall not attempt to cover the whole field today.
As far as international affairs are concerned there is nothing in the speech from the throne, except a few platitudinous sentences, to describe the sombre and, indeed, the dangerous situation which we face in the world. No ideas are put forward concerning ways in which we might meet these dangers and solve these problems except in a general and unimpressive way. There is no recognition of the fact that the menace of communist imperialism and colonialism is as great as ever-perhaps, in some respects, greater than ever. I think we are particularly conscious of that menace today as I speak on the forty fourth anniversary of the establishment of the independent republic of the Ukraine, the short lived and tragic history of which we all know. That history surely brings home to us that while overseas colonialism and imperialism of the older type is on the way out and has almost disappeared, the kind of colonialism which imperialistic communist powers impose by moving across adjacent borders to destroy ancient civilizations and subjugate their populations is stronger and more menacing than ever. It is not likely there will be real peace in the world-creative and constructive peace- until that type of colonialism is removed, too. I have no doubt that when the time comes we shall have a full debate on international affairs at which time we shall be able to examine why, among other things, Canada's


influence in these matters has declined rather than increased in the last four or five years.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If it is a foolish statement, as is stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs Mr. Green), may I say that it is being made by many objective observers of international matters today.
I am also very conscious of the fact that in dealing with the program in the speech from the throne I cannot be sure that I am dealing with the full government program or all the government proposals, owing to the fact that the Prime Minister has introduced into our constitution a new convention-and it is a very dubious one indeed- of making his own speech from the throne after the official one has been handed down and of including in that political speech of his own things which he thinks will perhaps get more credit for himself and for his party, as coming from him, than from any more exalted or objective source. He has done it more than once and for all I know he may be doing it today. That situation makes it difficult to introduce a debate on the speech from the throne when we do not know whether or not we have the full government program outlined in that speech.
However, as we have the program outlined in that speech, its declarations contain no call to national action; they make no challenge for a national response. They do not even seem to call for an early election.
On January 20 the Globe and Mail, a paper certainly not friendly to this party but traditionally very friendly indeed to the government, referred to the speech from the throne in an editorial entitled "An Uncertain Trumpet" as one with a "curiously thin and inadequate note". What an unhappy contrast, in content, inspiration and challenge, to President Kennedy's state of the union message a few days earlier.
One commentator has likened the program in it to a budget with the dollar sign thrown away completely, and this at a time when this year's budgetary deficit is likely to be $700 million or more, when our cash deficit is likely to be well over $1 billion and when we are told by the government that this is a time of expansion and moving forward. If the dollar sign is to be thrown away completely, as this prediction has it, I wonder whether the cheque writing machines are now ready for overtime work.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, we recall the words of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton). I am sorry that he is not in his place today and I regret even more the reason for his absence. I know that he is ill.

We all wish him a speedy recovery. However, we recall his words on November 29 1961, in Saskatoon-I happened to be in Saskatoon with him on the same day-when in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix he is reported as follows:
Today Hon. Alvin Hamilton, home from grainselling trips which have taken him half way around the world, said that there would be no farm acreage payments in this calendar year. He did not attribute this to lack of federal dollars but said that the cheque machines required to roll out the barrels of money were busy with other financial details.
It was therefore left for the Prime Minister a little bit later to make the announcement of acreage payments. Of course, that is the usual procedure followed by this government. The good announcements come from the Prime Minister and the hard and harsh announcements come from the other ministers, as was the case with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) when he had to speak within a few hours after the Prime Minister had spoken-I am thinking of New Brunswick and Fredericton-and had given no indication that the bad announcement was to come shortly from the mouth of the Minister of Public Works about the Chig-necto canal.

Now, in 1962, we have the ringing declaration in the speech from the throne that the matter is going to be submitted to a parliamentary committee.

Of course, the contributory insurance plan of the government comes to mind in that connection. Some promises are to pay out large sums of money on the eve of an election without saying how much; a railroad here or a railroad there; a bridge in Montreal without tolls or in Prince Albert a bridge to political resources; a ferry promised now for a causeway promised once and refused yesterday.
Perhaps the most notable thing about the speech from the throne is its omissions. Some of these notable and important omissions are explainable only by the characteristic inability of the government to make up its mind, never to do today what it can put off until tomorrow or, if a royal commission can be appointed, until a few years from now.
The Address-Mr. Pearson
Four main matters are omitted from the speech from the throne, in so far as any effective proposals for dealing with them are concerned. There is no program of action, although there are a few words, for the stimulation of economic growth, or even an indication of awareness of its necessity. Presumably-and I shall have something to say about that matter today-the government is quite satisfied with the economic growth we are experiencing at the present time. Second, there is no program of effective action to combat chronic unemployment, especially in certain areas. Third, there is no definition of a coherent policy indicting that the government recognizes the dramatic and important new trading patterns and policies that are now taking shape in Europe, and the opportunities and the challenges which these changes represent for this country.
Fourth, after two years of indecision and procrastination, confusion and contradiction, there is still no statement of an intelligible Canadian defence policy, especially whether Canada is or is not to have nuclear arms. This omission-and I should like to say a few words about it-merely confirms the shocking refusal of the government to make up its mind on defence policy, especially on the use of nuclear weapons. With all the confidential and secret information at its command, it delays, doubts and procrastinates. Yet it attacks the opposition, which has not the responsibility for policy and has never been given any of the confidential information on which policy must be based, for not finally and dogmatically laying down policy in this field. Could there possibly be a more complete abdication of governmental responsibility? The government spokesmen, when they speak-and let us remember that they speak with ministerial responsibility, each one of them-contradict each other and indeed they contradict themselves.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) agrees that nuclear warheads alone make sense for some of the arms we now have secured. Statements have been made confirming that these arms will have nuclear warheads, and other statements that they will not have them. Other statements have been made saying that no decision will be reached as long as the disarmament conference is proceeding or as long as there is a chance for a nuclear test ban or as long as there is no deterioration of the international situation. "We will make up our minds after these other things happen."
At the United Nations, on the other hand, reflecting presumably the view of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Canada voted for a resolution, opposed by most

Meanwhile, Mr. Speaker, we are spending millions on weapons, some of them already in the hands of Canadian forces, which will have only a minimum of effectiveness without nuclear warheads.

What he calls an exchange of washing resulted in the European six increasing their trade in 1960 over 1950 with the outside world by 23 per cent, and increasing their gross national product by 6.5 per cent in one year. When this minister or any minister talks about the high tariff walls of the European market, he forgets, or perhaps he never knew, that the European common market is averaging national tariffs at the level of January 1, 1957 and, as announced, is willing to reduce that average 20 per cent on the basis of reciprocal concessions. Indeed, this objective was announced two years ago when Dr. Hallstein was in Washington. Perhaps the government does not know that the United States has already negotiated that kind of deal with the European common market for important reductions in tariffs. Is this restrictionist? I wish the Minister of Agriculture were here to reply.
Is this Canadian government ready to bargain on that basis? Perhaps we will learn something about this during this debate. Will the government be so naive as to merely sit back and hope that it can get the benefits of negotiation by others? We do not know about this, but perhaps one of the ministers will tell us something about it.
Our own position in this matter, Mr. Speaker, is the belief that we should be in the forefront of this kind of negotiation, not following behind. Perhaps I may be permitted to do something I have very rarely, if ever, done in the house in order to indicate the consistency of the position we have taken. I should like to quote from a speech I made in January, 1958, on this very matter in Vancouver at the board of trade. I said this:
In Europe, six continental countries are prepared to form a customs union to be complemented by free trade arrangements with the United Kingdom and probably also the Scandinavian countries and the rest of continental Europe.
This has almost come about.
When these arrangements are completed, there will be a tendency in some parts of this large area to aim at European economic isolationism. These countries have tried to gain easier access to the United States and Canadian markets without any substantial degree of success and they may now feel that the only other alternative is a


large economic unit of their own, as self-sufficient as they can make it. That would be an unhappy development.
Indeed it would be tragic-politically and economically-if the free world should now divide into separate economic blocs while the Soviet world remained a massive, single, trading unit.
There is increasing evidence that Soviet leaders are more and more interested in conquest by economic methods, used and controlled by the same means and for the same purposes as are the diplomatic and military arms of that government.
The west is gradually-too gradually-recognizing this major shift in Soviet policy, and the necessity of taking steps to meet it. If declarations of interdependence from Washington and Paris mean anything, they must mean closer co-ordination of our economic and scientific activities in NATO. It will not be possible, in the long run, for allies to work together in close defence co-operation and grow increasingly apart in economic conflict.
If then we do not wish to weaken the western coalition: and if, in Canada, we do not wish either to face the United States alone or become too dependent economically on it, then surely the best policy for us is to seek economic interdependence within the north Atlantic community through freer trade. A first, and important step in this direction-and one certainly, in my view, which should be given careful, sympathetic, and detailed consideration-is the United Kingdom offer of free trade with Canada.
For Canada a north Atlantic area with the freest possible trade would certainly mean a much greater export market in the United States and in Europe; lower cost of production for many Canadian industries-and lower living costs, I would hope, for Canadian consumers.
Then, I add this paragraph, too:
In short, it seems that the era of gradual tariff reductions through GATT has come to an end. We do not surely wish to replace it by a western Europe and a North America aiming at selfsufficiency. If not, then surely the best alternative, and the best way to meet the Soviet economic and political challenge is an Atlantic freer trade area to complement the European customs union and free trade zone. For Canada, is this not the best way to reduce our economic dependence on the United States while expanding our trade, maintaining our economic development, and raising even higher our living standards?
This is a challenging prospect and is surely worth serious and immediate consideration, negotiation and planning. Could there be a finer initiative for Canada?
Mr. Speaker, that initiative was not taken by this government. There was the famous 15 per cent diversion which raised great expectations in the United Kingdom some years ago and which fell so flat. There was the free trade offer and the sterile response to that by this government.

The fact that preferences have been whittled away since the war has not been by our will but by the will of the commonwealth countries themselves. Look at what happened when John Diefen-baker became Prime Minister of Canada. He wanted to increase imports from Britain by 15 per cent. We were delighted. Consider the position of the United States administration as put forward by the under secretary of state, Mr. Ball. Listen to this excerpt from President Kennedy's state of the union message on January 11; I wish we could have had something like this in the speech from the throne. He said:
Will we in this country adapt our thinking to these new prospects and patterns-or will we wait until events pass us by?

That certainly applies to this country. Then the President went on to say, in the same speech:
Concessions, in this bargaining, must, of course, be reciprocal, not unilateral. The common market will not fulfil its own high promise unless its outside tariff walls are low. The dangers of restriction or timidity in our own policy have counterparts for our friends in Europe. For together we face a common challenge: to enlarge the prosperity of free men everywhere and to build in partnership a new trading community in which all free nations may gain from the productive energy of free competitive effort.

Perhaps I may be permitted to put on the record what we in this party said immediately with regard to the President's state of the union message. The proposal was made on January 11, 1962. We said this, and the statement was issued in my name:
President Kennedy's proposal for expanding trade is a farsighted program. It would have the active support and encouragement of a Liberal government in Canada. I believe that Canadians should be among the first to welcome such a policy, because of the great benefits that will flow from it.
The President is asking congress for authority to negotiate with the European common market to lower trade barriers through mutual concessions. We cannot tell how quickly the President's administration will be able to move on these lines. But I am sure that Canada should be encouraging the movement. Indeed, a Liberal government would have taken the initiative earlier. We would share fully in negotiations for expanding the trade with Europe of both the United States and Canada. We would also be interested in discussing U.S. proposals that would include the reduction of U.S. tariffs on Canadian products, which are an important barrier to our trade.
Above all, however, the United States proposal recognizes the need for maximum economic cooperation among the countries of the democratic world, in the face of the threat of communist expansion and aggression. Canada should be pressing forward, not holding back in these realistically farsighted efforts.

Then I went on to say:

The spring of 1961.
-we have experienced a normal economic upswing from the previous recession. Unfortunately, this improvement has so far been modest and slow. (2)	That the deduction from income by a taxpayer of expenditures incurred for advertising directed to the Canadian market in a foreign periodical wherever printed be disallowed.
It is the intention of the government to implement the first of these recommendations; that is to say, the government proposes, in due course, to prevent the importation of periodicals containing advertising that is primarily directed to the Canadian market. This will not in any way interfere with the continued importation into Canada of the many magazines that are printed and published
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker abroad and that carry advertising that is primarily directed to their own home markets. It will, however, prevent publishers of magazines in other countries from preparing, as a by-product, and sending into Canada, adaptations of their magazines in which they carry advertising directed to the Canadian market.
As for the second major recommendation of the report, it is the intention of the government to implement it but with an important modification. If this recommendation were implemented without a change the result would be not merely to prevent the future establishment in Canada of foreign-owned, foreign-edited periodicals, but to put an extremely heavy, they claim, burden on those which have already been established here. The latter, in that they import most, if not all, of their reading matter as a by-product of their parent magazines abroad, have an unfair competitive advantage over their Canadian competitors; and this advantage must be offset. On the other hand, they have established themselves in this country in good faith, they employ Canadian labour, and they attempt to supply Canadian readers with a specially adapted product.
Accordingly, in applying the recommendation that advertising placed in non-Canadian magazines be no longer deductible as an ordinary business expense for tax purposes, the government will introduce an important, although partial, exception. As a general rule, the recommendation will be applied, and this tax change is expected to make it unprofitable to initiate the publication of any new byproduct magazines in this country. However, there will be an amelioration in the case of non-Canadian magazines that are already, as of today, published and printed in Canada, and that are or will shortly be carrying on editing operations in this country. When Canadian advertisers place advertisements in these latter magazines, their advertising outlays will continue to be deductible expenditures to the extent of 50 per cent. In other words, half the burden proposed by the royal commission will be removed from those nonCanadian periodicals that have established their operations within this country.
Both these recommendations, that relating to imports of Canadian-directed advertising and that relating to advertising in non-Canadian magazines, are of a fiscal nature. I make this announcement now so that adequate time, in all fairness, will be given for all existing plans and contracts that are normal and reasonable to be completed.
Nevertheless, the announcement I am making at this time will give immediate encouragement to Canadian magazines. All advertisers interested in reaching the Canadian

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker market through the periodical press will, from today, be laying their plans in ways that will give greater and more assured support to the truly Canadian publications.

I am going to refer to the economic situation. They blame us for everything today. Internationally, it was a sordid picture. Economically, where was the country going, the Leader of the Opposition asked. Well I intend to make some references to recent press statements after having dealt in general with the economic situation within our country. The detail will be filled in by the Minister of Finance and others who will follow.
The hon. gentleman blamed us today for lower productivity per individual. That was a new accusation. According to him we are to blame because men today are not producing as much as they were producing per person four or five years ago. That is how far they have gone. I have been across this country and I have also listened to Canadian people everywhere. Do you know what I have heard? Over and over again it has been said to me that this perpetual groaning on the part of the opposition, this degrading of our country, has gone beyond what is reasonable and beyond what is regarded as the proper attitude to take in parliament. We want criticism. Criticism is of the essence of parliamentary government. But that dirge they chant, that funereal appearance they assume, and that attitude of gloom they adopt for their own personal glee, are things which the people are beginning to see through in the light of what has been done and the policies that have been followed by this government.
I will refer to some of the things that have been done, first generalizing on the Canadian economic scene today. Mention was made of the fact that elsewhere in the world everything was fine. I have simply to read what the President of the United States said the other day. He has also mentioned on a

number of occasions, that since the war there have been four or five recessions. He has mentioned the difficulty of these successive recessions, each followed by a shorter period of general prosperity. The other day he also stated that this year we have turned the corner and are on the way up. The opposition picture Canada as if it were a place by itself, with difficulties not found elsewhere. One has just to read the United States press week by week. There you find out the fact that they also face a situation similar to that which we have faced in Canada. As to Canadian economic activity, the pace of expansion has accelerated as the year progressed and as the economy continues to advance most economic indicators passed their previous peaks and were still pointing upwards as the year ended. National output rose significantly in both the second and the third quarters of the year, and the indications are that this trend continued in the final quarter of 1961. The quickening rate of business activity improved the labour situation and employment rose.
I might also point out that the strength of the current expansion is evident in the new records attained in such important fields as national output, industrial production, incomes, consumption and commodity exports. These are notable achievements in view of the fact that there was a partial failure of Canada's 1961 grain crop. The upswing has been unusually strong and broadly based. The significant feature of the upturn is the broadness of its scope and the extent to which the improvement has permeated the Canadian economy. Some Canadian industries achieved record output and sales in 1961. Others operated above their 1960 level. New annual production records were achieved by both the mining and manufacturing industries.
In connection with mineral production, there was an increase of approximately 2.8 per cent. There was also an increase in gas exports. As a result of the policies of this government in making possible a national policy, we have been able to achieve new records. New annual production records were also chalked up in primary steel and wood pulp. Cement shipments were higher by 6 per cent than they were in 1960 and constituted the second highest figure on record after 1958. The gross national product amounted to approximately $37 billion and there was a significant gain between the second quarter and the third quarter. The achievement of this gain is remarkable, again I point out, when consideration is given to the $300 million or $400 million decline in the grain crop when compared with that of 1960. If we had had an average grain crop in 1961, it

would have meant an increase of about per cent in the gross national product. However, the opposition just go on, Mr. Speaker, and wail and whine.
How greatly the foreign trade situation seems to worry, frustrate and annoy them. However, the improvement in Canada's foreign trade was one of the most encouraging economic developments in 1961. At the end of the first ten months of 1961 commodity exports stood at an all-time high. Imports were moderately higher than they were in 1961 and for the first time since 1952 Canada had a surplus in commodity trade. When we came into office there was a deficit in commodity trade of some $713 million. As a result of our policies, the encouragement of export markets and the action taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his officials, and those of the other departments of government, and by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) directly, the improved situation was brought about. The record level of exports was achieved largely by expanding foreign sales to countries other than our two traditional best customers, namely the United Kingdom and the United States. Sales to western Europe and Japan continued to expand during the year, and there were large exports of grain to communist countries.
I do not know what the suggestion was today on the part of the Leader of the Opposition. However, if he is criticising the sale of wheat to communist countries, I ask him to repeat that criticism in those areas of Canada which are particularly affected by the benefits that come from the export of that wheat.

We are not complacent about it. Neither are they complacent in the United States where their percentage of unemployment is higher than ours. They are adopting various policies to which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) will refer during the course of his remarks. We have been facing a situation within our country where unemployment is always seasonally higher than anywhere else and, in spite of the prophecies of the opposition, we are able to say at this time that in every month during the year there has been a comparative reduction in unemployment. They did not know that only European countries could belong as members. They suddenly changed their standpoint today and endeavoured to leave the impression that the United States was going to enter into something of this kind. I will quote President Kennedy's words:
I am proposing, in short, a new American trade initiative which will make it possible for the economic potential of these two great markets to be harnessed together into a team capable of pulling the full weight of our common military, economic and political aspirations.
I personally believe this, that in the years ahead the free world will have to come closer together than ever before, economically and politically, if we are to survive in freedom.
Then, what did the president say?
I am not proposing-nor is it either necessary or desirable-that we join the common market, alter our concepts of political sovereignty, establish a rich man's trading community, abandon our traditional most favoured nation policy, create an Atlantic free trade area, or impair in any way our close economic ties with Canada, Japan and the rest of the free world.
This has been our attitude. We have done everything to encourage Britain to place the viewpoint of Canada before the community, and it has been done.
As a result of the serious decision recently taken by the council of ministers of the common market, the Six have moved from the first stage to the second stage of the 12-year transitional period leading to the achievement of their economic community.

The position of the common market at the end of the fourth year is generally as follows: The Six have reduced tariffs among themselves by 40 per cent, and eliminated import restrictions, also amongst themselves, over a wide range. They have taken the first of three steps bringing their individual tariffs towards the level of their common external tariff. They have paved the way for common transport and commercial policies. They have made appreciable progress towards the free movement of labour, services and capital wtihin their community. That is one of the principles of the treaty of Rome, free ingress and egress of labour among the countries in the treaty area; complete freedom of access on the part of labour, that is, under the treaty. They have continued to develop closer political ties.
The government of Canada recognizes the implications of the common market. We understand the political and economic reasons which led to the creation of this economic community. While Canada has co-operated with its partners I make it clear that if the strengthening of Europe were to be achieved at the expense of the commonwealth, or other parts of the free world, we do not believe it would fulfill its promise. Canadian representatives have brought these considerations to bear in the discussions regarding European integration. I can say that so far as negotiations between the United Kingdom and the Six are concerned, the British position, stated by the Lord Privy Seal, is that the British government indicated their willingness to accept the broad lines of the Rome treaty as it is, and indicated they shared the political aims and objectives of the Six. Second, the political significance of the commonwealth and its contribution to strength and stability in the world were emphasized. He, I think,

made it clear that the safeguarding of commonwealth interests was the central consideration affecting the United Kingdom's decision to join.
We represent the government of Canada. We represent the people of Canada and, lest the result of what Britain was doing were to weaken the relationship within the commonwealth, were to place us in a detrimental position together with Australia, New Zealand and other countries of the commonwealth, then it is our responsibility to place that view before the British government. I can say the British government recognizes that Britain is at the centre of a world wide trading system and is aware that production facilities have been developed in many commonwealth countries to serve the British market.
Much of British industry in turn has developed on the basis of favourable access to markets in many parts of the world and the British government has, in the face of these considerations, indicated that commonwealth interests should be accommodated. It has given assurances to commonwealth governments that this would be a crucial feature of the negotiations. This was our concern, as I pointed out a moment ago, not the attitude of trying to say to a sovereign nation within the commonwealth "You shall not do this." We were concerned with the protection of our trade. We realized how much was at stake. We consider-and the British fully understood this and understand it now-that they should be provided with the fullest information on the implications for Canada, because only in that way could the British negotiators be aware of all the factors that have to be taken into account to safeguard those interests.
When I hear hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the house talking about Canada's stand against Britain and the commonwealth I must remind them that the foundation of the Conservative party is close relationship with the British commonwealth. That was our foundation when it was an empire and that has continued to be the foundation ever since. That is the position of this party and, despite whatever representations the opposition make to the contrary, our relations with the commonwealth are close and will continue to be so.
We hold that we are entitled to consultation and by that I mean the fullest consultation. Consultation is more than the reporting of what has been done. I have repeated on a number of occasions, and I think there has been some general support for my view, that when the negotiations have finally arrived at a point as between the United

Kingdom and the countries of the European community, then in that spirit which at all times actuates the members of the commonwealth, we should meet together in a commonwealth prime ministers' conference and there talk over the matter in the light of our common dignity and the maintenance of the strength of this body of free countries all over the world, which has so much to contribute to peace. It is naturally agreed that before the final decision is taken the fullest consultation is of first importance, and in the past I have expressed my hope that, while all the countries are not in agreement, it would be possible that such a prime ministers' conference might be held in Canada.
Since becoming Prime Minister and attending such meetings I have advocated that although most of the meetings of the prime ministers should take place in London, from time to time, but not in rotation, there should be meetings throughout the commonwealth thereby implementing the concept of the equality of each member within that family.

You will remember in 1957 and 1958, when we spoke of the need to develop our northern areas. That idea and view were ridiculed as being a policy of development from igloo to igloo. I look back over that period and think of the plans we brought into effect. One has only to travel in the north of Canada to see the tremendous changes that have taken place. In the provinces we also made provision for co-operation in the provincial development of all things designed to bring about a strong economic development in every part of our country, the development of our national resources, the development of our northern regions, urban redevelopment, transportation and communication development, and a balanced regional economic development as practiced through the Atlantic provinces grants.

We have launched a tremendous power policy with the assistance of the provinces. We are hoping that with regard to the Columbia river agreement between the province

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker and the federal government can be reached so that the treaty may be brought before the present session.

The greatest need in the years ahead, as I see it, will be the assurance of power to all parts of Canada. It is for that reason that in the speech from the throne we make provision for the beginnings of action which we hope will bring about the establishment of a national power grid in all parts of Canada. Manitoba has already approached us in this regard; other provinces are interested. My hope is that we shall make progress, to the end that in this respect Canada will not fall behind but will be in the forefront in the maintenance of such necessary things as the provision of power to all parts of our country, assuring a new equality of development in every part of our country.
There is one other matter in the province of Quebec that is receiving our attention in this development plan which covers all the provinces of Canada. That is the reference of the Richelieu-Champlain waterway project to the international joint commission. The opposition, when in government, gave this matter little or no attention from 1937 on. We felt some action should be taken and we have given serious consideration to proposals for the improvement of this waterway.
On September 8, 1961 I pointed out to the house that when the examination had been completed and a decision had been made as to the proper course to be adopted, the house would be made aware of that decision immediately. On December 18 the government announced its decision to refer this matter to

In the development policy for agriculture in all parts of our country, agriculture in eastern and western Canada has received every consideration from this government. Indeed, as I examine the expenditures that are made for agriculture in eastern and western Canada in connection with support prices and all other matters that enter into that field, I find that on a per capita basis there is a high degree of equality in all parts of the country.

The answer was always the same, and it was always in the negative. In 1958 we brought into effect acreage payments and I know what the reaction was. I am not going to harass anyone or cause any wounds to be opened but I remember the description "peanuts". All I can say is that I have travelled in western Canada and that is not what the small farmers say. All through the years there have been requests in western Canada for a fair and reasonable price approaching parity with regard to that portion of the wheat sold in Canada for domestic purposes. The sum of $40 million was made available in 1958 and again, two years later, in 1960 which in fact brought to the farmers of western Canada a price equivalent to a parity price in respect of that wheat consumed in Canada.
We intend this year again to bring into effect a similar system whereby farmers will receive the same amount as in 1960. Mention was made by someone-I believe it was the Leader of the Opposition-that the Minister of Agriculture had stated that the payment would not be made in the calendar year, that the cheque machinery was working too slowly and it would be impossible to do it. Exactly what the Minister of Agriculture meant was that we were sending out cheques to the western farmers in respect of wheat through P.F.A.A. and there would be no payment made during the calendar year 1961. There is nothing unreasonable about that statement. One thing this government has done has been to see to it that when farmers find themselves in difficulty, whatever part of Canada they live in, they receive that consideration which in the past was so often denied.
When I said a moment ago that our policy was for other parts of Canada, too, I think of what we have done in connection with tobacco. I also think of what we have done in connection with sugar. I have before me an editorial which appeared in the Chatham daily News on December 2 under the heading "New Sugar Policy is Welcomed by Growers". It reads:
Details of the federal government's new Canadian sugar policy have been made public and do not need to be recapitulated. Under this program the new support will be given to sugar beet growers starting with the 1962 crop.
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
The article goes on to indicate what private members can do and ends by saying that credit is due to the hon. member for Kent, Ont. (Mr. Danforth) for his persistent efforts.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And while that hon. member is named in his own paper, the same applies to all the members supporting the government in western Ontario.
Now I come to the question of social security. Among the most important measures forecast in the speech from the throne are those relating to old age pensions. We already have in Canada four major government systems for providing for old age pensioners as well as numerous private pension plans. Therefore it is desirable that the house and the public should understand how the measures referred to in the address affect this program.
The four matters to which I refer include first, a government annuities plan, which is used by a great many individuals and groups as a foundation for their security. We propose to retain this important feature and hope it will continue in the future to be as useful as it has been, whatever additional pension measures may be introduced. The second, in point of time, is what is now the Old Age Assistance Act. Under this an old age pension is provided jointly by the provincial and federal governments to persons who are in need as determined by a means test applied by the province in accordance with both provincial and federal law. It is not generally known that this payment of old age assistance is contributed to by the federal government on a 50-50 basis. This pension looks after those who have been unable to provide for their own old age and who need a pension before the age at which the universal pension is payable.
We propose that the amount of the pension should be increased and we believe that the economic capacity of this country warrants the benefit of an increased scale for our old people who are in need. The cost of doing this will, of course, rest on the budget and, as is the case with regard to all these measures, will ultimately be met by the Canadian people through their taxes. The third of this pensions group is the old age security pension payable as of right to persons at 70 years of age without regard to need. As in the case of old age assistance, the government has reached the conclusion that it can and should ask Canadians to accord a higher priority to the welfare of older Canadians than in the past and to pay pensions on a higher scale than heretofore.
In creating a complete system of providing for retired persons which will be made out

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker of all the measures, due regard should and will be had to the levels of these old age security pensions financed by the special levies under the act.
A fourth element which is often overlooked is provision for aid under the Unemployment Assistance Act. Under this act parliament provides, through provincial and local authorities, half the money required for the payment of what is widely termed public assistance or relief. I would point out here that if the new policy of the new Liberal party as enunciated by the Leader of the Opposition in Quebec city is brought into effect, that is the kind of joint expenditure which will be ended.
Under the Unemployment Assistance Act, parliament is now sharing in the payment of substantial amounts to old people as well as to other people who are unemployed or unemployable for various reasons.
These are the four plans for dealing with old age pensions. There are now hundreds and possibly thousands of private pension plans which have become an important and integral part in employer-employee relations in Canada. Usually these plans are financed by contributions of employers and employees. These are normally recognized under income tax arrangements which permit contributions to these plans to be free of taxes but which impose taxes if they are payable on the pension payments themselves if they exceed the exemptions on the taxpayer's income. The new feature that will be proposed to parliament will be to add to this system. It will enable the structure to be completed in addition to an increase in the amount of payments for old age pensions.
We find that there are still a good many people who wish to have greater provision made for their old age, and who are able and willing to contribute to such retirement pensions but who are not covered either by government annuities, by private pension plans or registered retirement saving plans. In order to complete the structure for old age pensions it is necessary that parliament should have the authority to enact a statutory system of old age pensions and related survival and disability benefits that would be comparable to that under the modern British and United States legislation in the nature of benefits that could be provided.
At the present time parliament's authority derives from section 94A of the British North America Act which permits it to make laws in relation to old age pensions so long as they do not affect the operation of provincial laws. This constitutional authority does not permit parliament to enact a plan which would include benefits payable under specified circumstances to the widows and children of
fMr. Diefenbaker.]
contributors or to contributors who become disabled before they are old. To extend the law in this most desirable way it would be necessary to secure constitutional authority. With this idea in mind I have written to the premiers of all the provinces asking their concurrence in an amendment to section 94A of the British North American Act. I should like to table a copy of the letter to Premier Robarts of Ontario. The text of the others is similar. If the house is willing, the letter could be appended to Hansard.

speechtext: Agreed.

In His Excellency's speech reference was made to the desirability of the new plan taking into account private pension arrangements and the need for portability of pension rights. I should like to make it clear that pension rights under this type of national plan would be portable. On the other hand, we must contemplate private plans remaining in operation. Pension rights under them should be made portable, if necessary by the passing of either provincial or federal legislation. Our plan should take these private plans into account and should not require additional contributions by those already contributing under satisfactory private arrangements.
I have taken note of the proposal made public recently by the Leader of the Opposition, or by the Liberal party, for the payment of additional contributory pensions. At this time I am not going to outline the deficiencies or the weaknesses of palatable sections which when examined are found to be hollow and shallow. However, I feel it necessary to note that the plan contemplates no change in the constitution and no extension of benefits to dependants of contributors nor to disabled contributors. We feel that any plan limited in this way would be most seriously deficient.
As I set out in the letter to the various premiers of the provinces, believing that this is something which should be done we are going to ask parliament to consider the necessary amendment. Ever since the Clark report came in we had been hoping that the provinces would be able to come to an agreement on the question of having our constitution amended in Canada or of patriating the constitution. However, while progress has been made in that regard, we now feel that what we undertook to do in 1958, and have intended ever since to do, on the basis of an amendment to be passed in the parliament of Canada is now impossible. We believe this change

should be made now. As it will take further time to reach agreement on the method of amendment of the constitution in Canada, we intend to proceed by way of an address to the Queen requesting the amendment to be made by the parliament of Westminster and have asked the various provinces to concur in that request. When we have been able to secure that amendment, over and above the old age pension paid and the increase which we intend to place before parliament, there will be in effect a pension system contributed to by the people of Canada to the end that there will be available for all Canadians, on a portable basis, pensions in keeping with their needs and also with their ability to to make payment.
First, there will be a reasonable and fair old age pension. We have shown our feelings in this regard by adding to the $6 provided or introduced by the previous government, a further increase of $9. When I proceed tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, with the concluding portion of my remarks, I shall deal with this matter somewhat further. Then there are two other matters I wish to deal with because the Leader of the Opposition covered them and I wish to assure him that all the information asked for by him will be furnished.

subtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT-LETTER TO PROVINCIAL PREMIERS RESPECTING OLD AGE PENSIONS

speechtext:
Ottawa, January 17th, 1962.
The Honourable John P. Robarts, Q.C., M.P.P.,
Premier of Ontario,
Toronto, Ontario.
My dear Premier:
My colleagues and I in the federal government have come to the conclusion that the Canadian social security system should be improved by the addition of a plan for graduated old age pensions on a contributory basis in addition to the basic old age security pension, for all those who can reasonably afford additional provision for their old age and who have not already undertaken it under private pension plans or other contractual arrangements. We believe that a plan of this kind, which would have some resemblance to the American social security laws and the recent British legislation, should also contain provisions for the payment of benefits under certain circumstances to the widows and children of contributors who die, and to former contributors who become permanently disabled.
The British North America Act was amended in 1951 by the addition of the following as section 94A:
"It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, but no law made by the parliament of Canada in relation to old age pensions shall affect the operation of any law present or future of a provincial legislature in relation to old age pensions."
The law officers of the crown advise me that this authority would permit parliament to enact a contributory, graduated old age pension plan but would not permit the inclusion of benefits payable under certain circumstances to widows and children, nor to contributors who become disabled before they are old. To extend the law in this most desirable way, it would be necessary to replace the present section with one reading as follows:
"94A. It is hereby declared that the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to
(a)	old age pensions, and
(b)	pensions and other benefits incidental to, or conducive to the better operation and administration of, a scheme of old age pensions,
but no law made by the parliament of Canada under the authority of this section affects the operation of any law enacted by the legislature of a province in relation to any of the matters specified in paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section".
My colleagues and I had hoped that agreement would have been reached by this time on a means of amending Canada's constitution in Canada and that this change in section 94A would have been one of the first amendments made under the new arrangements. It is now evident that it will take some further time to reach agreement on the methods of amendment of the constitution in Canada and it will therefore be necessary to proceed by way of an address to the Queen, as in the past, requesting that the amendment be made by the parliament at Westminster. I am writing therefore to ask that you concur in a request for an amendment to section 94A of the British North America Act in the form proposed above.
Yours sincerely,
John G. Diefenbaker
Tuesday, January 23, 1962
